newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unveils details of proposed tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils details of proposed tax cuts.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Sunday released details of its proposal for nearly $100 billion in tax cuts through the year 2002.
Many of the cuts are aimed at helping middle class families pay their bills, raise their children, send them to college, upgrade their skills and save for retirement, it said.
- A phased-in $500 tax credit for dependent children, phased out for taxpapers with adjusted gross income between $60,000 and $75,000. Total five-year cost: $46.7 billion.

- Education and training tax incentives costing $38.6 billion. They include HOPE scholarship tax credits of up to $1,500 per year and a phased-in $10,000 tax deduction for post-secondary school education. The former costs $18.6 billion and the latter, $17.6 billion.
- Expanded Individual Retirement Accounts. The moves, which will cost $5.5 billion, including a doubling of the income limits on the accounts and expanded penalty-free withdrawals.
- Capital gains tax relief for home sales. This will cost $1.5 billion and allow taxpayers to exclude $500,000 of capital gains from the sale of a principal residence.

- Tax incentives for distressed areas, costing $2.4 billion. Among the proposals: a "brownfields" initiative to encourage companies to clean up abandoned, contaminated industrial properties and $100 million worth of credits for investors in community development banks.
- Welfare-to-work initiative. This would provide a temporary tax credit to employers who hire long-term welfare recipients and would cost the government $500 million.
- Small business and farm estate tax relief, costing $700 million.

The Clinton tax-cut plan, which will be contained in the budget he formally submits to Congress on Thursday, would also extend a number of tax credits that are set to expire, including one for research and development.

It would also provide some $560 million worth of tax benefits to the computer software industry and some $260 million of Wasahington, D.C. tax incentives to encourage the employment of city residents and revitalise distressed areas.
